newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-AUSTRIA AND AMERICA WIN FIRST GOLDS.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-AUSTRIA AND AMERICA WIN FIRST GOLDS.

text.p: Hilary Lindh of the United States and Renate Goetschl of Austria won their countries' first gold medals of the Alpine skiing world championships on Saturday.

Lindh, an outsider, continued a north American tradition by winning the women's downhill while Goetschl sprang another surprise by conquering the combined event to restore Austria's badly dented national pride.
Switzerland's Heidi Zurbriggen took silver in the downhill ahead of Sweden's Pernilla Wiberg. Germans Katja Seizinger and Hilde Gerg were second and third in the combined.
Goetschl recaptured for her country a title they had not won since Annemarie Moser-Proell in 1978. The two Austrians have often been compared with each other.

"To win gold is incredible. I knew I had a good chance but this is not only good for me, it's good for the whole team." said Goetschl, whose team mates have been pilloried at home by a national media that had expected great things.

The big loser of the day, if a silver medallist can be termed as such, was reigning Olympic downhill champion Seizinger who had been a favourite in both events after finishing runner-up in the super-G earlier in the week.
"It's been a frustrating day," said Seizinger after finishing just 0.04 seconds behind Goetschl in the combined and fifth in the downhill.
"I gave my best but it wasn't good enough. I'm disappointed because both races were influenced by the weather.
"Twice I lost by a few hundredths of a second. I'm especially disappointed with the downhill."
The combined downhill had been postponed twice because of high winds and snow and the regular downhill was moved forward to allow both races to be held in succession on Saturday.
"I was convinced at the start that it would not be an ordinary race," said Goetschl of the combined.
"After the downhill I thought 'Oh no, today won't be a good day'. Both Katja and I were unlucky this morning because the sun came out after us and the slope became faster."

Gerg, who won bronze in the super-G, said she had been furious at the start of the combined downhill because the wind picked up just before her. "I thought at first I had no chance but obviously now I am happy. I have two medals and that's more than I expected."

Lindh, who has not finished in the top three of any World Cup race this season, started 14th in the downhill and stunned everyone with a time of one minute 41.18 seconds that ended Italy's run of three golds in three women's races.
"I'm just in shock right now," she said.

Wiberg was one of the happiest medallists, redeeming a disappointing championships after two golds last year. It was the first medal of her career in a speed discipline after winning five golds in technical and combined events.

Lindh, the 1992 Olympic downhill silver medallist who last won a race in 1994, followed in the wake of 1996 downhill champion and compatriot Picabo Street -- absent this year due to injury -- and 1993 champion Kate Pace of Canada.
"I thought maybe I could win a medal but I didn't know I could be first," said the 27-year-old Lindh, who won a bronze in the discipline last year in Sierra Nevada.
"I guess when I race big events I get excited."
Lindh had considered retiring at the end of last season, then opted to continue although probably only for one further year on the circuit.
"I was so close to not racing this year," she said. "Even at the start of the season I didn't know if I had made the right decision."
